Observed facts: a previously well teenage boy had two weeks of upper‑respiratory and sinus symptoms, then four days of severe retro‑orbital headache. He trained 3–5 hours daily in a 12‑foot pool, performing breath‑holds at depth without compressed air, and reported a forehead pop and pain while at depth. Initial treatment was for sinusitis. He returned with fever 39.2 °C, pulse 103/min, forehead and periorbital swelling worse on the right. Labs: WBC 7.6×10⁹/L, CRP 7.3 mg/L, ESR 31 mm/h. CT demonstrates a frontal sinus abscess with a subperiosteal collection; no intracranial or orbital extension is shown. MRI for marrow involvement has not been performed. Drainage results, cultures, and outcome are unavailable.

Hypotheses: the initial sinusitis diagnosis now represents a complicated frontal sinusitis with subperiosteal abscess (Pott’s puffy tumor) rather than simple sinusitis. The training history raises the possibility of barotrauma‑induced mucosal injury facilitating bacterial invasion, but causation is unproven.

CT establishes the presence and extent of a frontal sinus abscess and subperiosteal collection, but it does not exclude intracranial extension, orbital involvement, or osteomyelitis of the frontal bone.

Proposed immediate actions: obtain urgent ENT and neurosurgical consultation; arrange MRI with contrast to assess intracranial and marrow involvement; start broad‑spectrum intravenous antibiotics covering Staphylococcus aureus, streptococci, and anaerobes; plan surgical drainage of the sinus and subperiosteal abscess; monitor neurologic status and repeat imaging if clinical deterioration occurs.
